Preparation of the laser-induced graphene (LIG)
Two  glass  slides  were  prepared  as  the  initial  substrate  for  LIG  (laser-induced  graphene)  and  Ag-coated  LIG 
samples. Kapton tape was attached to the slides using double-sided adhesive (Fig. 1a). The surface of the polyimide 
was cleaned with alcohol-soaked cotton to remove any contamination. Before graphene synthesis, optimizing 
the  parameters  of  the  samples  under  different  conditions  is  crucial.  The  laser  must  have  sufficient  power  to 
break the carbon bonds in the polyimide without damaging the graphene structure. Uniformity and graphene 
formation throughout the polyimide film require proper resolution adjustment. Laser writing was tested at levels 
ranging from 20% to 55%. Finally, the optimum power of 28% was selected as the most suitable power for both 
the bare and silver-coated samples to form graphene (Fig. 1b). Graphene synthesis was successfully performed 
on all three samples, and it was of good quality after adjusting the parameters of the laser system, including 
power, speed, resolution, and focal length. The samples were subjected to LIG treatment using a GCC LaserPro 
C180 II machine capable of producing laser irradiation with a power of 40 W.

Characterization  tests,  including  Raman  spectroscopy,  SEM,  EDS,  FESEM,  and  TEM  imaging,  were 
performed to quantitatively and qualitatively investigate the structure of LIG and to interpret the distribution of 
silver nanoparticles within the nanocomposite sensor.

Sputter coating of silver and preparation of PDMS nanocomposite film
Silver was deposited on the Kapton substrate after the laser-induced graphene (LIG) process, ensuring effective 
integration of the silver nanoparticles with the laser-induced graphene (Fig. 1c). To achieve this, the sample was 
placed in a Desk Sputter Coater DSR1 vacuum deposition system and coated with silver for 300 seconds. The 
coating process was controlled solely by the sputtering duration. Since the coating thickness was not directly 
essential, the coating time was adjusted by measuring the sheet conductance of the silver-coated LIG samples. 
After  300  seconds  of  sputtering,  the  sheet  conductance  did  not  change,  indicating  complete  coverage  and 
adequacy of the coating process. This is discussed in detail in33–35.

After sputtering, Sylgard 184 PDMS polymer from Dow Corning was used to create a polymer substrate with 
the desired mechanical properties. For this purpose, the PDMS resin was combined with the crosslinker at a 1:10 
ratio by hand for 10 minutes. To remove bubbles, the mixture was placed in a desiccator connected to a vacuum 
pump to remove all trapped air. A plexiglass mold, not shown in the figure to highlight other components, was 
attached to the glass with double-sided tape to enclose each sample completely (Fig. 1d). These molds, designed 
with precise dimensions and sealed completely, must be used to ensure the uniformity of the polymer thickness 
throughout the mold and the maintenance of the composite film’s uniformity. Before pouring the polymer into 
the molds, the glass with the attached samples was placed on a perfectly level surface. The oven was also leveled 
before placing the samples inside. The samples were placed in the oven, and the location of the samples was 
leveled. The samples were then cured at 70°C for two hours (Fig. 1e). After curing and removing the samples 
from the oven, some time was allowed for the glass and mold to cool entirely before facilitating the separation 
process. Then, the mold was separated from the polymer with a surgical blade, and then the molds were gently 
removed from the glass with a spatula. Finally, the nanocomposite film was peeled off from the samples (Fig. 1f) 
to provide the final nanocomposite sensor (Fig. 1g).

Each synthesized sensor element was cut to standard dimensions, and the resulting linear strain behavior 
was evaluated using tensile testing (5 cm in length and 5 mm in width). The strain sensing performance of strain 
sensors can be fully characterized by factors including stretchability, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, response 
and recovery time, and dynamic durability. Initially, the initial resistance of each element was measured by a 
multimeter and then placed in a tensile testing machine. Cyclic test parameters such as cyclic test type, number 
of cycles, applied strain level, and initial length were set in the appropriate software to use the desired tensile test 
for the samples.

thickness and its geometric pattern). The sensitivity of the sensor element is evaluated by a parameter called the 
gauge factor, or GF for short . According to the definition, the gauge factor is the response of the relative change 
in electrical resistance to mechanical strain and is calculated using the following equation36,37:

www.nature.com/scientificreports

Silver-decorated laser-induced 
graphene for a linear, sensitive, 
and almost hysteresis-free 
piezoresistive strain sensor

Fatemehsadat Abedheydari1, Sadegh Sadeghzadeh1, Mohammad Saadatbakhsh1,2, 
Amirhossein Heydariyan1 & Elnaz Khakpour1

A new approach has recently emerged in graphene synthesis by direct laser writing (LIG), which is 
highly economical and scalable, unlike previous methods. Here, the sputtering method has been used 
to coat silver onto the laser-induced graphene-based sensor. The results demonstrate that the chosen 
approach substantially impacts the expected outcomes. The initial resistance values were consistent 
across the different sensor samples. The average resistance was slightly lower in the silver-coated 
samples compared to the uncoated samples, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Ag coating in 
enhancing the electrical conductivity of the LIG material. However, the difference in resistance was not 
statistically significant. The electromechanical behavior of the Ag-coated LIG strain sensor was tested 
under cyclic tensile strain. The gauge factor increased from 12.9-14.7 for the uncoated LIG sensor to 
17.2-26.7 for the Ag-coated sensor, with the difference growing at higher strains. At 5%, 30%, and 
70% strain, the gauge factor increased by 30%, 80%, and 82%, respectively. Sensors measuring 1-70% 
strain were developed, enabling use in various applications. Blood pulse measurements showed 
the silver-coated sample produced more uniform and reliable results than the uncoated sample. 
The number of beats matched a commercial pulse oximeter. This sensitivity, linearity, and reliability 
demonstrate the potential for commercializing these sensors.

Keywords  Laser-induced graphene, Silver decorated, Graphene, Wearable electronic, Strain Sensor

In recent years, based on nanotechnology achievements, various flexible strain sensors have been developed that 
convert  mechanical  properties-dependent  variables  (such  as  stretching,  bending,  and  torsion)  into  electrical 
signals.  These  wearable  electronic  devices  can  monitor  human  health  status  in  real-time  and  accurately  by 
receiving  various  biological  or  physiological  stimuli.  Advanced  composite  materials  and  new  manufacturing 
processes have led to the production of unique devices tailored to specific healthcare applications (e.g., human 
motion detection1, heart rate2, blood pressure2, respiration3, sports activity monitoring4, smart textiles5, and soft 
robotics6). In addition, composite sensors are resistant to degradation due to the wide range of materials and 
innovative manufacturing methods. Unlike conventional sensors, they have a particular tensile behavior and 
sensitivity.

However, given the widespread use of these sensors, several essential requirements and considerations must 
be considered. To better monitor signal complexity, the strain sensor must be sufficiently flexible and highly 
sensitive, have a wide measurement range, be fast-response capable, have excellent durability, and be compact.

Traditional  commercial  wearables,  mainly  in  the  form  of  glasses,  watches,  wristbands,  or  belts,  are  made 
entirely or partially of flat, stiff materials that require rigid supports or additional flexible straps to be attached 
to the human body. Therefore, clinical devices that use existing wearables can cause discomfort and limit the 
laboratory’s  monitoring  of  human  physiological  data.  This  significant  limitation  must  be  overcome  despite 
the growing market for wearables in broader screening outside the lab. Therefore, bulky and stiff plastics and 
metal  parts  in  sensors  and  electronics  must  be  replaced  with  skin-like  materials  to  increase  wearability  and 
performance. Specifically, such electronics provide stable and compliant contact with soft human skin without 
adding additional mechanical or thermal loads or causing skin breakdown. Current development approaches 
for advanced wearable, flexible hybrid electronics (WFHE) focus on soft and flexible form factors, non-irritating

and non-toxic properties, fully autonomous energy components, integrated wireless communications, and cost-
effective processes7. It should be noted that these complex features must be designed to meet the demanding 
requirements of advanced physiological recording from the human body.

Conductive polymer composites (CPCs) have been used as strain-sensing materials due to their advantages 
of being lightweight, low cost, good processability, high sensitivity, and environmental compatibility7. They have 
created  new  opportunities  for  fabricating  high-performance  strain-sensing  devices  cost-effectively.  In  CPC-
based  strain  sensors,  the  change  in  conductive  networks  under  applied  strain  produces  an  output  electrical 
signal,  enabling  them  to  detect  external  stress  stimuli.  To  improve  the  properties  mentioned  above,  various 
strategies are employed in the fabrication of CPC strain sensors:

•  Modulating the ratios of conductive fillers
•  Incorporating hybrid fillers into a polymer matrix
•  Functionalizing the surface of conductive fillers
•  Tailoring the orientation and distribution of conductive fillers

Composite sensors have two main parts: 1) a polymer matrix and 2) a conductive filler. The conductive fillers 
create a continuous conductive path in the polymer matrix, which is responsible for the electrical and mechanical 
properties of the sensor that transfer mechanical stimuli to the conductive network.

In this context, piezoresistive sensors with a mechanism for converting applied strain into electrical resistance 
have been used in applications to monitor structural changes. One of the popular polymers in this field used 
as the substrate for these sensors is a thermoset polymer called polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)8. It has unique 
properties such as transparency, non-fluorescence, non-toxicity, biocompatibility, stable thermal and chemical 
properties, unique physical properties, and high flexibility. PDMS has no adhesion to polymer layers, an essential 
advantage for its application in MEMS and biomedical technology9.

Graphene  is  a  promising  material  for  fillers  due  to  its  exceptional  properties,  such  as  high  electrical 
conductivity and desirable mechanical strength10. Researchers have reported producing porous graphene using 
laser irradiation, namely laser-induced graphene (LIG). The ability to rapidly synthesize graphene foam using 
the LIG method has revolutionized the fabrication and production of sensors incorporating graphene as a filler 
material. This method has advantages such as being simple, low-cost, and suitable for producing graphene over 
a  large  area11.  This  method  produces  LIG  patterns  in  a  non-contact  process  via  direct  laser  engraving  on  a 
polyimide (PI) film. In terms of piezoresistive performance, the changes in the pore size of the LIG foam, the 
electrical contact between its walls, and the quantum tunneling phenomenon create significant sensitivity in the 
sensor.

Hybrid nanomaterials
Nanomaterials with different dimensions, such as silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), silver nanowires, gold nanowires, 
graphene, carbon black, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs), can be combined with graphene using various deposition 
methods12–18. This approach helps maintain high conductivity under various strains and excellent stability.

Graphene is a two-dimensional structure consisting of a single layer of the carbon honeycomb lattice. Due 
to its exceptional electrical conductivity, carrier mobility, and mechanical properties, graphene has become a 
unique material. This new solid-state system is a suitable substitute for the next generation of advanced micro 
and  nanoelectromechanical  devices.  Therefore,  it  has  attracted  unprecedented  attention  in  fundamental  and 
applied research.

Graphene  can  be  produced  using  methods  such  as  mechanical  exfoliation  of  graphite,  chemical  vapor 
deposition  on  metals  from  hydrocarbon  gas  precursors,  thermal  decomposition,  and  reduction  of  graphene 
oxide. Laser irradiation of a polymer precursor to induce photochemical and thermal conversion to graphene is 
another method for producing graphene. Graphene obtained in this way is usually called laser-induced graphene 
(LIG) or laser graphene (LSG). LIG has a slightly lower quality than graphene obtained by other methods, but 
relative simplicity and low cost are the main advantages of laser induction.

The surface morphology of LIG is characterized by a complex and inhomogeneous porous pattern resulting 
from the rapid production of gases during irradiation and the sp3→ sp2 carbon conversion, an example of a 
flat graphene structure. The inhomogeneous structure is also due to defects in the regular arrangement of C 
atoms,  as  5-  or  7-membered  carbon  rings  can  be  found  that  slightly  bend  the  regular  hexagonal  network19. 
LIG’s  composition  and  morphology  and  its  electrical,  mechanical,  and  surface  properties  depend  on  factors 
such as the type of laser and the processing parameters. With precise control of laser parameters during the laser 
scribing process, graphene is obtained in porous and nanofiber-organized structures. LIG generally has high 
graphene conductivity, large specific surface area, strain, and corrosion resistance and can also be functionalized 
to catalyze reactions or sense strain, temperature, magnetic field intensity, and chemical concentration20.

Unlike  traditional  synthesis  routes  based  on  the  thermal  decomposition  of  resins  at  high  temperatures 
(around 1200 °C) in an inert atmosphere, the laser line enables the fabrication of porous carbon structures by 
performing in situ synthesis on a polymer substrate and patterning in the form of fully customizable electrodes 
and circuits.

Polyimide (PI) films
Polyimide (PI) films are readily available in sheets, rolls, and even tapes with a wide range of thicknesses and are 
the first and most popular precursor substrates for LIG production. PI is also widely used to produce flexible 
electronics due to its high strength and chemical and thermal stability. The chemical structure of PI appears to 
be particularly suitable for LIG production, as 2sp aromatic carbons are more prone to form hexagonal graphene 
structures than other precursors that only produce amorphous carbon.

Laser irradiation of PI
Irradiation of polyimide with UV laser pulses, when the laser fluence is 100–500mJ/cm2, causes local heating at 
the target spot and increases the surface temperature to 1700 °C. These results are further supported by molecular 
dynamics (MD) simulations, which show that the conversion to LIG occurs at high pressure and temperature. 
The energy available is sufficient to break down C-N, C-O, C-H, and C-O19,21–23.

The  D3  structure  is  more  sensitive  to  similar  strain  than  the  flat  structure.  Similarly,  the  sensor  can  be 
designed  with  a  corrugated  structure  to  improve  sensitivity. The  corrugated  structure  allows  the  stress  to  be 
concentrated on the indentations when the sensor is stretched, and the resistance will change significantly24.

Sensor composition
Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a thermoset polymer, is the most/one the most commonly used sensor substrate 
due to its unique properties, including transparency, non-fluorescence, non-toxicity, biocompatibility, stability 
in thermal and chemical conditions, unique physical properties, and flexibility.

This polymer is a neutral, non-toxic, and non-flammable silicone elastomer with a leading O-Si chain and a 
repeating Si(CH3)2O unit. Its molecular weight generally varies from 10 to 60 thousand grams per mole, and its 
specific gravity ranges from 0.91 to 1.0025–27.

PDMS has a mineral backbone with organic groups as pendants, classified as a "semi-mineral" or "organo-
mineral" polymer. PDMS and silica composites have relatively high impact strength, determining a material’s 
ability to resist sudden fracture force. Using standard impact tests, such as the Charpy pendulum and drop weight 
impact  tests  on  PDMS  composites,  it  has  been  concluded  that  the  impact  strength  increases  with  increasing 
PDMS  content  in  a  composite28.  It  behaves  like  an  elastomer  because  the  glass  transition  temperature  of  its 
siloxane component is much lower than at room temperature. As a result, it can absorb large amounts of energy 
during impact testing and delay crack and fracture formation28,29.

The  graphene-based  composite  has  excellent  electrical  properties  because  the  contacts  between  platinum 
nanoparticles and the graphene network create many conductive tunnels. Notably, the experimental results show 
high sensitivity (GFmax = 489.3) and a broad strain range of up to 20% of the platinum/graphene composite 
matrix after deposition on a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) substrate, which shows a significant performance 
compared to the LIG strain sensor on a polyimide substrate without platinum nanoparticles. Porous graphene 
with a large surface area can be formed by photochemical reactions and the photothermal effect introduced by 
ultraviolet laser. The surface of graphene flakes is rough with granular textures, resulting from the rapid pulsed 
laser process. The TEM image shows that the nano-sized platinum particles are homogeneously distributed on 
the graphene sheet30. It initially increases with increasing platinum loading and then decreases with increasing 
platinum content to 2.0 mmol. The gauge factor was 45.6 at (0–6%), 269.5 at (6–16%), and 489.3 at (16–20%) 
at a platinum concentration of 1.0 mmol. It is also worth noting that the hysteresis in the device was primarily 
suppressed with the addition of 1.0 mmol of platinum30.

The rational combination with highly conductive graphene may limit the electrical conductivity of the 2MoS-
LIG  nanocomposite.  Still,  the  intrinsic  active  hierarchical  structure  of  2Mos  and  the  synergistic  interaction 
between the composite layers reduce the fracture of graphene nanosheets to certain strain limits31. Laser scribing 
of a few-layered 2Mos coated on commercial PI film using a CO2 infrared laser creates 3D porous graphene 
decorated with MoS2, which enables superior electromechanical properties. The high-sensitivity sensor response 
(GF = 1242), low hysteresis, ultra-low detection limit, wide working range, and long-term reliability (over 12000 
cycles) were demonstrated.

Considering  the  advantages  of  the  LIG  method  in  sensor  manufacturing,  such  as  scalability  and  cost-
effectiveness, although the graphene obtained by this method has a similar quality to other laboratory methods 
with a slight decrease in electrical properties, with techniques such as hybridization with secondary nano-fillers, 
creating micro-cracks and manipulating the sensor geometry, a significant increase in the basic properties of 
the sensor can be made. The primary novelty of the current approach lies in the application of silver decoration 
via sputtering to enhance the performance of laser-induced graphene (LIG) strain sensors. This is crucial for 
accurate measurements in various applications, as it allows the sensor to detect even small changes in strain 
with high precision. Moreover, the silver decoration enhances the stability of the sensor under cyclic loading 
conditions, addressing common challenges faced by other graphene-based sensors. This improved stability and 
reliability are essential for the long-term performance and durability of the sensor in real-world applications. 
Here,  the  sputtering  method  has  been  used  to  coat  silver  onto  the  laser-induced  graphene-based  sensor. 
Considering sputtering’s capability at various penetration depths, this approach offers significant advantages, 
including  precise  control  and  high  design  flexibility.  Sputtering  was  studied  before  and  after  laser  treatment 
to investigate the effect of silver coating on the fabricated sensors, resulting in optimal conditions. The results

Preparation of the laser-induced graphene (LIG)
Two  glass  slides  were  prepared  as  the  initial  substrate  for  LIG  (laser-induced  graphene)  and  Ag-coated  LIG

the  parameters  of  the  samples  under  different  conditions  is  crucial.  The  laser  must  have  sufficient  power  to 
break the carbon bonds in the polyimide without damaging the graphene structure. Uniformity and graphene 
formation throughout the polyimide film require proper resolution adjustment. Laser writing was tested at levels 
ranging from 20% to 55%. Finally, the optimum power of 28% was selected as the most suitable power for both 
the bare and silver-coated samples to form graphene (Fig. 1b). Graphene synthesis was successfully performed 
on all three samples, and it was of good quality after adjusting the parameters of the laser system, including 
power, speed, resolution, and focal length. The samples were subjected to LIG treatment using a GCC LaserPro 
C180 II machine capable of producing laser irradiation with a power of 40 W.

Sputter coating of silver and preparation of PDMS nanocomposite film
Silver was deposited on the Kapton substrate after the laser-induced graphene (LIG) process, ensuring effective 
integration of the silver nanoparticles with the laser-induced graphene (Fig. 1c). To achieve this, the sample was 
placed in a Desk Sputter Coater DSR1 vacuum deposition system and coated with silver for 300 seconds. The 
coating process was controlled solely by the sputtering duration. Since the coating thickness was not directly 
essential, the coating time was adjusted by measuring the sheet conductance of the silver-coated LIG samples. 
After  300  seconds  of  sputtering,  the  sheet  conductance  did  not  change,  indicating  complete  coverage  and 
adequacy of the coating process. This is discussed in detail in33–35.

After sputtering, Sylgard 184 PDMS polymer from Dow Corning was used to create a polymer substrate with 
the desired mechanical properties. For this purpose, the PDMS resin was combined with the crosslinker at a 1:10 
ratio by hand for 10 minutes. To remove bubbles, the mixture was placed in a desiccator connected to a vacuum 
pump to remove all trapped air. A plexiglass mold, not shown in the figure to highlight other components, was 
attached to the glass with double-sided tape to enclose each sample completely (Fig. 1d). These molds, designed 
with precise dimensions and sealed completely, must be used to ensure the uniformity of the polymer thickness 
throughout the mold and the maintenance of the composite film’s uniformity. Before pouring the polymer into 
the molds, the glass with the attached samples was placed on a perfectly level surface. The oven was also leveled 
before placing the samples inside. The samples were placed in the oven, and the location of the samples was 
leveled. The samples were then cured at 70°C for two hours (Fig. 1e). After curing and removing the samples 
from the oven, some time was allowed for the glass and mold to cool entirely before facilitating the separation 
process. Then, the mold was separated from the polymer with a surgical blade, and then the molds were gently 
removed from the glass with a spatula. Finally, the nanocomposite film was peeled off from the samples (Fig. 1f) 
to provide the final nanocomposite sensor (Fig. 1g).

Each synthesized sensor element was cut to standard dimensions, and the resulting linear strain behavior 
was evaluated using tensile testing (5 cm in length and 5 mm in width). The strain sensing performance of strain 
sensors can be fully characterized by factors including stretchability, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, response 
and recovery time, and dynamic durability. Initially, the initial resistance of each element was measured by a 
multimeter and then placed in a tensile testing machine. Cyclic test parameters such as cyclic test type, number 
of cycles, applied strain level, and initial length were set in the appropriate software to use the desired tensile test 
for the samples.

the piezoresistive response is relatively linear and modest. However, as the strain increases from 5% to 10%,

but at a much slower rate. The saturation of the piezoresistive response can explain this behavior. As the strain 
increases further, the material may reach a point where the response becomes more stable and less sensitive

The  observed  differences  in  performance  between  the  Ag-coated  and  uncoated  LIG  sensors  can  be 
attributed to several physical mechanisms. The silver coating enhances the electrical conductivity of the LIG 
material, primarily due to the formation of conductive pathways provided by the silver nanoparticles. This is 
because the presence of metal nanoparticles can significantly improve the charge carrier mobility and reduce 
the  overall  resistance  of  graphene-based  materials.  In  this  study,  the  gauge  factor  of  the  Ag-coated  sensors 
increased significantly compared to the uncoated sensors, indicating a higher sensitivity to strain. This increase 
can be explained by the interaction between the silver nanoparticles and the LIG matrix, which enhances the 
piezoresistive effect. As strain is applied, the silver nanoparticles can redistribute and create additional conductive 
pathways, leading to a more pronounced change in resistance. Furthermore, the porous structure of the LIG 
allows for better adhesion and distribution of the silver nanoparticles, which contributes to the sensor’s overall 
stability and sensitivity. The increased LIG surface area and defect sites also facilitate better electron transfer, 
which is crucial for the piezoresistive response. In summary, the combination of enhanced conductivity from the
